name: Tagabawa
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 6 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: DuBois, Carl D. & Lauretta J. DuBois. 2006. Phonemic Statement of Tagabawa. 1st ed. Manila: Summer Institute of Linguistics Philippines. 19 pp. ISBN 978-971-18-0406-0. SIL Language & Culture Archives entry 35849 (data 1987-88, Malasila, Makilala, Cotabato).
catalog_quote: The analysis of stress is based on a corpus of more than 2,600 Tagabawa words. An additional 600 words were excluded from analysis as being borrowed from Spanish, English or Cebuano Visayan. Stress consists of an increase in intensity and a raising of pitch. Stress also consists of vowel length in open (CV) syllables. Of the Tagabawa corpus of polysyllabic words, stress occurs as follows: on penultimate syllables: 92% (approximately 2400 words) on ultimate syllables: 8% (approximately 200 words) on antepenultimate syllables: less than 1/2 of 1% (8 words) Although stress is predominantly penultimate, it is phonemic, as evidenced by the following minimally and nearly minimally contrastive pairs of words. [ˈʔaːtod˺] /ˈʔatod/ ‘look at’ [ʔaˈtod˺] /ʔaˈtod/ ‘stump’ [ˈkaːpi] /ˈkapi/ ‘hawk’ [kaˈpiː] /kaˈpi/ ‘coffee’ [taˈgaːnaʔ˺] /taˈganaʔ/ ‘prepare’ [tagaˈnaʔ˺] /tagaˈnaʔ/ ‘orig.people’ [ˈpaːlad˺] /ˈpalad/ ‘palm of hand’ [paˈlad˺] /paˈlad/ ‘while’ ... [ˈʔənda] /ˈʔənda/ ‘where’ [ʔənˈdaʔ˺] /ʔənˈdaʔ/ ‘didn't’ Vowel length occurs only in open (CV) stressed syllables. There are no word pairs that differ only by vowel length.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.citation: DuBois, Carl D. & Lauretta J. DuBois. 2006. Phonemic Statement of Tagabawa. 1st ed. Manila: Summer Institute of Linguistics Philippines (SIL Language & Culture Archives entry 35849), 19 pp.
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (19 pp., PDF metadata 'Tagabawa Phonemics', created 2006-10-19; text is garbage, so I rendered p. 10 to an image and read it directly). Section '2. STRESS' begins mid-page on 'Page 10 of 19' and ends at the foot of that page (p. 11 starts '3. DISTRIBUTION'). The quoted passage is there verbatim: 'The analysis of stress is based on a corpus of more than 2,600 Tagabawa words. An additional 600 words were excluded.. borrowed from Spanish, English or Cebuano Visayan. Stress consists of an increase in intensity and a raising of pitch. Stress also consists of vowel length in open (CV) syllables. Of the Tagabawa corpus of polysyllabic words, stress occurs as follows: on penultimate syllable…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is contrastive (phonemic) but heavily skewed: in a corpus of >2,600 native polysyllabic words it falls on the penult in 92%, on the final syllable in 8%, and on the antepenult in 8 words; a stressed open syllable is lengthened, but length is never independently contrastive. Eight (near-)minimal pairs penult vs. final are given.
new_statements.exceptions: 8% final-stressed words and 8 antepenult-stressed words (all native); about 600 loans from Spanish, English and Cebuano were excluded from the count. Grammar Essentials (1991, p. 4) and Tagabawa Texts (2005, p. 2) add only that stress is phonemic and left unwritten in the orthography.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation/lexical forms (wordlist corpus); vowel length tied to open stressed syllables. Sentence intonation is described separately in Grammar Essentials §6.1 (high pitch on the stressed syllable of the last word). The 1892 Gisbert dictionary prologue notes accent on the syllable preceding a geminate consonant (penult), consistent with the modern default.
new_statements.identity_note: The deciding source describes Tagabawa as spoken in Sitio Lambac, Malasila, Makilala, (North) Cotabato, and states it is assumed to hold for the whole language (Kidapawan to Toril, south of Mt Apo); only /l/~/r/ regional variation is noted. Same languoid as Glottolog taga1272 (ISO bgs). It is distinct from Guiangan/Klata 'Bagobo' (gian1240), which the authors explicitly separate; Gisbert 1892's 'Bagobo' (Sibulan/Tibbison/Tuban, Davao) is tagged Tagabawa by Project Gutenberg/DuBois.

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog record (DuBois & DuBois 2006 §2: stress phonemic, 92% penultimate / 8% final / <0.5% antepenultimate, minimal pairs 'kapi~ka'pi, 'ʔatod~ʔa'tod, ta'ganaʔ~taga'naʔ, 'palad~pa'lad): the online edition marks exactly these pairs by stress alone (kapi 1/2, atud 1/2, taganà 1/2, palad 2 [paˆlad] 'while') and supplies a stress mark almost only for non-penultimate words (324 final vs 11 penult among 361 marked of 5,809), the lexical pattern the 2006 percentages describe. It adds no prose rule (the Phonology page of the site is still unread, hand-download list) and does not touch the standing Zorc 1978 disagreement held by the project. Compared with the 2016 PDF we hold export…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The part of the online edition that could be read (all 5,809 entries) contains no prose statement on stress; the site's Phonology page is unread. The entries themselves mark stress lexically: 361 of 5,809 headwords carry a pronunciation field in which 'ˆ' precedes the stressed syllable; counting vowel nuclei after the (last) mark, 324 mark final stress, 11 penultimate, 17 antepenultimate (mostly Spanish loans: kantidad, imbistigar, pasinsiya, ganansiya), 8 are phrases and 1 is a prose note; i.e. pronunciation is supplied essentially only where stress is not the default penultimate, and homographs are distinguished by stress alone (apun 1 [aˆpun] 'pubic hair' vs apun 2 [ˆapun] 'to perch'; atud 1 [aˆtud] 'stump' vs atud 2 [ˆatud] 'to observe'; kapi 1 [kaˆpi] 'coffee' vs kapi 2 [ˆkapi] 'kite'; taganà 1 [tagaˆnà] 'the original people' vs taganà 2 [taˆganà] 'to prepare'; also guyud, kani, pirit, tagad, taman, baliyan). This is the dictionary-side reflex of the catalog record: stress phonemic (lexical), predominantly penultimate with a marked final-stressed minority.
new_statements.secondary_stress: nothing: one mark per word; reduplicated forms carry one mark per member (gaˆbi-gaˆbi, suˆlit-suˆlit, taˆgad-taˆgad, buˆngónbuˆngón), i.e. each member keeps its own stress; no statement on secondary stress
new_statements.exceptions: none stated in prose; antepenultimate marks fall mostly on Spanish/Cebuano loans (kantidad, karintadur, imbistigar, pasinsiya, ganansiya, kulihiyu) and on a few native trisyllables marked at the word start (ˆbaliyan vs baliˆyan 'value', ˆbanuwa, ˆdaruwang, ˆgimpuruk, ˆsambilà, ˆsangkalì); the one prose note in a pronunciation field is góbbó: 'the stem-final vowel does not change when suffixed'
new_statements.identity_note: Tagabawa (Bagobo) of Malasila, Makilala, Cotabato and the Mt Apo area, Mindanao, as documented by Carl D. and Lauretta J. DuBois (SIL, fieldwork from 1970s-80s); the Webonary site publishes their FLEx lexical database (5,809 entries as of the 2024-03-13 upload), the 2016 PDF (SIL 66656) an earlier export of the same database.

sources.citation: DuBois, Carl D. & Lauretta J. DuBois. 1991 [1986]. Tagabawa Grammar Essentials. Manila: Linguistic Society of the Philippines & SIL (ms. dated 17 Dec 1991), 41 pp. SIL archives entry 43888.
sources.note: Introduction/orthography (p. 4): 'Although stress is phonemic, it has not been marked as such in the language examples cited throughout this description.' Section 6.1 (p. 24): in statements high pitch falls on the stressed syllable of the last word of the sentence, low pitch on the final (post-stress) syllable; questions raise pitch on the penultimate syllable of the final word.
